identification.summary: TunnelSnake is the name of an espionage campaign, and by extension the actor behind it, documented by Kaspersky in 2021. It centred on a previously unknown Windows rootkit named Moriya, a passive backdoor that lets operators covertly monitor network traffic and send commands to compromised hosts [S2]. Kaspersky described the campaign as active since 2019, with a small number of victims, reported by secondary coverage as about ten diplomatic entities [S3][S6]. Moriya is described as the successor of IISSpy, a rootkit seen in 2018 in attacks unrelated to the TunnelSnake campaign [S3][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: campaign active since 2019 (oldest Moriya instances dated October 2019); an older Moriya version appeared in a 2018 standalone attack, so activity may date to at least 2018 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: TunnelSnake is a Kaspersky campaign/cluster name. Kaspersky did not map it to a named group; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is known to this record. Coverage links the tooling developers to the authors of ProcessKiller, but this is a tool link, not a group merge [S3][S6]. Facts here come from secondary coverage; the Kaspersky Securelist report was not opened (see gaps).

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky did not attribute the attacks to a specific adversary. A Kaspersky researcher said both targets and tools connect to known Chinese-speaking groups, suggesting the actor is likely Chinese-speaking [S2][S3]. No government attribution is cited.
attribution.basis: Kaspersky assessment based on targets and tooling: a mix of custom tools and open-source malware commonly used by Chinese threat actors, plus a link between Moriya developers and ProcessKiller authors [S2][S3][S6].

objectives: Kaspersky assessed the purpose as espionage, while noting it lacked visibility into any data actually siphoned [S2].

targeting.notes: Secondary coverage (SOC Prime) says about ten prominent diplomatic entities in Africa and Asia were targeted; an exact victim count was not confirmed [S3][S6]. Kaspersky said attackers likely entered via vulnerable public-facing web servers; in one case the China Chopper web shell was used to infect an organization's mail server [S2].

capabilities.summary: Moriya is a rootkit with a kernel-mode driver and a user-mode agent. The agent loads the unsigned driver by abusing a VirtualBox driver to bypass driver signature enforcement. The driver uses the Windows Filtering Platform to inspect incoming traffic and pick out the actor's C2 packets; Moriya does not connect out to a server but waits for incoming traffic [S2][S6]. Other tools cited in a summary of Kaspersky's findings include the China Chopper web shell, BOUNCER, TRAN, Termite and Earthworm [S6]. ProcessKiller, used to shut down antivirus products, is linked to the same developers [S3][S6].

campaigns.name: Earlier Moriya version / IISSpy
campaigns.summary: An older Moriya version appeared in a standalone 2018 attack, and IISSpy, its predecessor, was seen in 2018 in attacks unrelated to TunnelSnake.

campaigns.name: Operation TunnelSnake
campaigns.summary: Oldest Moriya instances dated to October 2019 on networks of regional diplomatic organizations in Asia and Africa; activity continued through 2020.

campaigns.name: Kaspersky public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky published the TunnelSnake and Moriya findings and a press release; press coverage followed.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed to a named group; Kaspersky judges a Chinese-speaking actor likely [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Moriya rootkit, VirtualBox-driver abuse to load an unsigned driver, China Chopper, BOUNCER, TRAN, Termite, Earthworm, ProcessKiller [S2][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Covert C2 channel carried over incoming traffic filtered by the Windows Filtering Platform; specific servers and domains were not found in the sources gathered [S2][S6].
diamond.victim: About ten diplomatic entities in Asia and Africa (count not confirmed) [S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage against diplomatic bodies; Kaspersky saw ties to Chinese-speaking groups but made no state attribution [S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web and mail servers, and Windows hosts allowing driver loading [S2][S6].

gaps: The Kaspersky Securelist primary report was not opened; all facts come from search summaries of press coverage and Kaspersky's press release listing. Verify against the primary report, including the exact victim count.
Source dates for S1 to S3 and S6 are month-level and partly inferred (S1 date from the URL); confirm exact publication dates.
No actor name, sponsor or government attribution is available; overlap with named Chinese groups is not established.
Specific indicators, C2 infrastructure, victim identities and exfiltrated data are unknown.
Termite, Earthworm and BOUNCER usage is from a secondary summary only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web and mail servers at diplomatic and government organizations are key terrain, as they were the likely entry points [S2]. STEP 2: Kernel-mode rootkit stealth and passive C2 (no outbound beaconing) reduce the value of network-egress detection [S2][S6]. STEP 3: Template is web-server compromise via web shell, tunneling tools, then Moriya rootkit for long-term persistence [S2][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume espionage against diplomatic targets in Asia and Africa. MDCOA is use of the same driver-abuse technique against defense or coalition partners in the region. Candidate indicators: unexpected web shells on IIS or mail servers, VirtualBox drivers loaded on hosts without VirtualBox, unsigned kernel drivers, and Windows Filtering Platform filters not tied to known software [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation and coalition diplomatic networks in Asia and Africa as likely targets [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: kernel-level hunting and host forensics on partner or contractor systems need owner consent and proper authority. (3) Mission assurance: patch and harden public-facing web and mail servers and enforce driver blocklists [S2][S6]. (4) Coordination: share Kaspersky-derived indicators with partners and cyber defense providers, noting attribution is unconfirmed.
